episode_title: Why the Markets Are Pricing AI Wrong | Gavin Baker

real_qa.q: Why is NVIDIA trading at its lowest forward PE in the last 10 years despite accelerating AI demand metrics?
real_qa.r: NVIDIA is at its lowest forward PE of the last 10 years because the market believes the company is significantly over-earning. However, underlying fundamentals including GPU availability, rental pricing, spot price of DRAM, token growth, and operating cash flow from hyperscalers like Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon have all accelerated. Despite AI demand metrics showing consistent acceleration across all measured data points, the market has been selling off AI stocks due to concerns around credit financing, China's DUV capabilities, and open source model competition.
real_qa.requete: NVIDIA forward PE lowest 10 years why

real_qa.q: What is driving GPU rental price increases despite expectations they would decline in 2024-2025?
real_qa.r: GPU prices, contrary to all 2024 and 2025 expectations, are still rising vertically in 2026. Companies signed long-term contracts expecting prices to decline slowly or precipitously, but the contracted base of installed compute is now trading at massive discounts to the current spot market. As old long-term contracts roll off and compute gets repriced higher, operating cash flow will accelerate. One startup mentioned renting Blackwell clusters at mid-$2 per GPU hour in early months and now paying just under $4 per GPU hour seven months later, representing a 50-60% increase.

real_qa.q: How are hyperscaler operating cash flows accelerating despite market concerns about AI infrastructure financing?
real_qa.r: Operating cash flow from Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon accelerated from 28% to 32% year-over-year, and 35% when adjusted for unusual one-time items like EU legal expenses and fines. If hyperscalers monetize new Blackwell and Rubin chip capacity at rates even modestly above Ampere (two generations behind current capability), this generates 2 trillion dollars in operating cash flow, removing 700 billion dollars of credit financing demand. This acceleration is happening right as the market focused on credit risk, suggesting the buildout can be funded primarily through operating cash flows rather than debt.

real_qa.q: Why did the market interpret Meta's plan to rent compute capacity as negative despite no CapEx cuts?
real_qa.r: When Meta announced it would rent out compute capacity, the market interpreted this as very bearish and expected CapEx cuts. However, Meta did not cut CapEx. What actually happened was that Meta saw SpaceX sell optimized trading clusters at massive premiums to contracted rates and recognized the same opportunity. Meta's telemetry on CapEx plans showed no shift and continued getting more aggressive. Shortly after, Meta also released Llama 1.1, described as the best model in a long time, contradicting any narrative of reduced AI investment.
real_qa.requete: Meta compute rental CapEx negative market reaction

real_qa.q: How does open source model growth affect AI infrastructure demand and compute margins?
real_qa.r: Open source models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi shifted the token mix from expensive frontier model tokens with 80-95% inference margins toward open source alternatives. While this reduces margin dollars for frontier model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, it does not reduce overall compute demand because all tokens require identical amounts of computing resources. Open source effectively transfers margin dollars from frontier model providers directly to the AI infrastructure layer where cloud providers charge the same amount for compute, so total demand for infrastructure remains unchanged or increases due to the margin elasticity effect.
real_qa.requete: open source models compute demand infrastructure margins

real_qa.q: What is the primary factor that would reverse the current bullish AI infrastructure outlook according to Gavin Baker?
real_qa.r: If operating cash flow does not continue to accelerate, that would be negative. This acceleration depends on how Anthropic, OpenAI, Grok, Cursor, and open source models perform in driving token demand growth. Additionally, if there were a sustained dramatic contraction in GPU prices making it easy to acquire GPUs, that would also be worrisome. Baker emphasized he has not heard anyone say they have too many GPUs, suggesting GPU scarcity remains a fundamental constraint.
real_qa.requete: AI infrastructure demand collapse scenarios operating cash flow

guest.bio_context: Gavin Baker is an investment analyst and commentator who has been spending time in Silicon Valley analyzing AI infrastructure fundamentals and demand signals from private companies. He has developed detailed frameworks around GPU pricing, hyperscaler cash flows, and the financing dynamics of AI infrastructure buildouts.
